cards.front: What is the equation for photosynthesis?
cards.back: 6CO2 + 6H2O + light → C6H12O6 + 6O2

cards.front: Where does photosynthesis take place in a plant cell?
cards.back: In the chloroplasts

cards.front: Which pigment absorbs light in photosynthesis?
cards.back: Chlorophyll, which absorbs mostly red and blue light
Flattened membrane sacs inside the chloroplast where the light reactions of photosynthesis occur
A stack of thylakoids in the chloroplast
The fluid inside the chloroplast where the Calvin cycle takes place

cards.front: What are the products of the light reactions?
cards.back: ATP, NADPH and oxygen

cards.front: Where does the oxygen released in photosynthesis come from?
cards.back: From the splitting of water (photolysis)

cards.front: What does the Calvin cycle do?
cards.back: Uses ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide into sugar

cards.front: Which enzyme fixes carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle?
cards.back: Rubisco
Attaching CO2 to RuBP in the chloroplast to make organic molecules
Pores in the leaf epidermis that let CO2 in and water vapor out

cards.front: Which cells control the opening of stomata?
cards.back: Guard cells
Loss of water vapor from leaves, which pulls water up the xylem

cards.front: Which tissue carries water up from the roots?
cards.back: Xylem

cards.front: Which tissue carries sugars around the plant?
cards.back: Phloem, by translocation
Rubisco binds oxygen instead of CO2, wasting energy from photosynthesis

cards.front: How do C4 plants reduce photorespiration?
cards.back: They fix CO2 first in mesophyll cells and concentrate it in the bundle sheath cells
Plants that open their stomata at night to save water, e.g. cacti

cards.front: What is the role of the cuticle?
cards.back: A waxy layer that reduces water loss from the leaf

cards.front: Which factors limit the rate of photosynthesis?
cards.back: Light intensity, CO2 concentration and temperature
A cluster of chlorophyll and proteins in the thylakoid membrane that captures light

cards.front: What does photosystem II do in the chloroplast?
cards.back: Splits water and passes electrons to the electron transport chain
Making ATP in the chloroplast using the energy of light

cards.front: What is the role of NADP+ in photosynthesis?
cards.back: It accepts electrons to become NADPH

cards.front: What are the main parts of a leaf?
cards.back: Cuticle, epidermis, mesophyll, vascular bundle and stomata

cards.front: What is the function of the palisade mesophyll?
cards.back: It contains many chloroplasts to absorb light for photosynthesis
Yellowing of leaves due to a lack of chlorophyll, often from iron or nitrogen deficiency

cards.front: What is the main source of nitrogen for a plant?
cards.back: Nitrate taken up from the soil by the roots

cards.front: What is the role of root hairs?
cards.back: They increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals
Division of the nucleus that produces two genetically identical daughter cells
Division that produces four haploid cells, each genetically different

cards.front: What are the stages of the cell cycle?
cards.back: G1, S, G2 and the mitotic phase
The cell grows and copies its DNA before mitosis
DNA replication, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids

cards.front: What happens in prophase of mitosis?
cards.back: Chromosomes condense and the spindle begins to form

cards.front: What happens in metaphase of mitosis?
cards.back: Chromosomes line up along the middle of the cell

cards.front: What happens in anaphase of mitosis?
cards.back: Sister chromatids are pulled apart toward opposite poles

cards.front: What happens in telophase of mitosis?
cards.back: Nuclear envelopes re-form and the chromosomes uncoil, and the cell then divides
The division of the cytoplasm that splits the cell in two
The region where sister chromatids are joined

cards.front: What is the mitotic spindle made of in mitosis?
cards.back: Microtubules, which attach to the kinetochores
A protein structure on the centromere where spindle fibres attach
Organelles that organize the microtubules and form the spindle poles
A control point where the cycle can stop if something is wrong

cards.front: What does the G1 checkpoint check in the cell cycle?
cards.back: Cell size, nutrients and DNA damage
Proteins that activate kinases to drive the cell cycle forward
Stops the cycle for DNA repair or triggers apoptosis
Programmed cell death

cards.front: How does cancer relate to the cell cycle?
cards.back: Cells ignore the checkpoints and divide without control
Exchange of segments between homologous chromosomes in prophase I of meiosis

cards.front: Why does meiosis give genetic variation?
cards.back: Crossing over and independent assortment

cards.front: What is the difference between haploid and diploid?
cards.back: Haploid cells have one set of chromosomes, diploid cells have two
A pair, one from each parent, with the same genes
Chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis, giving the wrong number in the gametes
An extra copy of chromosome 21

cards.front: How do plant cells divide the cytoplasm?
cards.back: By forming a cell plate

cards.front: How do animal cells divide the cytoplasm?
cards.back: A cleavage furrow pinches the cell in two
A pair of homologous chromosomes joined together in prophase I of meiosis
A resting state where the cell has left the cell cycle
How prokaryotic cells divide, with no spindle or mitosis
One version of a gene
The combination of alleles an organism has
The observable trait that results from the genotype
The allele that shows in the phenotype when present
The allele that shows only when two copies are present
An individual with two different alleles of a gene
An individual with two identical alleles of a gene

cards.front: What does a Punnett square show?
cards.back: The possible offspring of a cross and their probabilities

cards.front: What was Mendel's law of segregation?
cards.back: Each parent passes on only one of its two alleles
Alleles of different genes are sorted into gametes independently
Crossing an unknown dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive
The heterozygote shows a blend of the two phenotypes
Both alleles are fully expressed, as in AB blood

cards.front: Which blood group alleles are there?
cards.back: IA, IB and i
A trait whose gene lies on the X chromosome

cards.front: Why are males more often colour blind?
cards.back: The gene is on the X and they have only one copy
Someone who has one copy of a recessive allele but shows no trait
A family tree used to trace how a trait is inherited
A change in the DNA sequence
A change of a single base
Three bases in mRNA that code for one amino acid
Copying a gene's DNA into mRNA
Building a protein from the mRNA at the ribosome
Builds new DNA strands during replication
A section of DNA that codes for a protein
The first generation of offspring from a cross
A cross that follows one gene
A cross that follows two genes, with a 9:3:3:1 ratio
One gene masks the effect of another
Genes close on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together
